# Uncovered Global Secondary Indexes

Nov 13, 2022, Kadir Ozdemir, Motivation and High Level Design  
Nov 28, 2022, Kadir Ozdemir, Detailed Design

This document provides the motivation and design details for strongly consistent uncovered global secondary indexes. 

# Motivation

Phoenix currently supports only strongly consistent covered indexes. Covered indexes can serve queries by itself and provide the best read performance for queries but can add significant overhead for write intensive workloads. This is because covered indexes require reading existing data table rows and two-phase commit writes to update indexes. The design presented here introduces uncovered indexes that do not require reading data table rows or two phase commit writes to update indexes during data table writes but still provide strong consistency. By doing so uncovered indexes reduce the write overhead drastically but require joining back index rows with their data table rows to serve queries. The increase in read latency for this join operation are justified for the improvement in write latency for write intensive workloads and batch updates via upsert select queries.

Although uncovered indexes will be slower than covered indexes during read operations, they will still improve the query performance for most use cases (when their performance is compared to the performance of data tables without indexes). It is clear that if the selectivity of a query is high (that is if the number of rows selected by the query is a small fraction of all rows), uncovered indexes will perform better than data tables. To improve the performance of uncovered indexes in the case where selectivity is not high, [PHOENIX-6501](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-6501) introduces server side batching for the join operation of the data table rows with index rows. This is done by buffering lots of data table row keys in memory (32K row keys by default),  and using a skip scan filter and multiple threads to issue a separate scan for each data table region in parallel. This will reduce the cost of joining and thus improve the performance.

# High Level Design

An index can be called an uncovered index if the index cannot serve a query alone. The sole purpose of an uncovered index would be identifying the data table rows to be scanned for the query.  This implies that the DDL for an uncovered index does not have the INCLUDE clause.   
Then an index is called a covered index if the index can serve a query alone. Please note that a covered index does not mean that it can cover all queries. It just means that it can cover a query. A covered index can still cover some queries even if the index DDL does not have the INCLUDE clause. This is because a given query may reference only PK and/or indexed columns, and thus a covered index without any included columns can serve this query by itself (i.e.,  without joining index rows with data table rows). Another use case for covered indexes without included columns is the count(\*) queries. Currently Phoenix uses indexes for count(\*) queries by default.

Since uncovered indexes will be used to identify data table rows affected by a given query and the column values will be picked up from the data table, we can provide a solution that is much simpler than the solution for covered indexes by taking the advantage of the fact that the data table is the source of truth, and an index table is used to only map secondary keys to the primary keys to eliminate full table scans. The correctness of such a solution is ensured if for every data table row, there exists an index row. Then our solution to update the data tables and their indexes in a consistent fashion for global secondary indexes would be a two-phase update approach, where we first insert the index table rows, and only if they are successful, then we update the data table rows, as shown below.

![][image1]

This approach does not require reading the existing data table rows when mutations include indexed columns, which is currently required for covered indexes. Also, it does not require two-phase commit writes for updating and maintaining global secondary index table rows. Eliminating a data table read operation and an RPC call to update the index row verification status on the corresponding index row would cut down index write latency overhead by at least 50% for global uncovered indexes when compared to global covered indexes. This is because global covered indexes require one data table read and two index write operations for every data table update whereas global uncovered indexes would require only one index write. For batch writes, the expected performance and latency improvement would be much higher than 50% since a batch of random row updates would not anymore require random seeks on the data table for reading existing data table rows.  
[PHOENIX-6458](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-6458), [PHOENIX-6501](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-6501) and [PHOENIX-6663](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-6663) improve the performance and efficiency of joining index rows with their data table rows when a covered index cannot cover a given query. We can further leverage it to support uncovered indexes. 

For deleting a data table row, we use a three-phase approach, as shown in the following diagram. In the first phase, we read the data table row to be deleted, and form the row key for the corresponding index table row. In the second phase, we delete the data table row. If successful, then we delete the index table row. Again, if this three-phase approach fails at the second or last phase, the data table row can be deleted, but the corresponding index row stays intact. However, again, this does not pose a correctness issue since we use an index table only to map index rows to data table rows. If the map points to a non-existent data table row, then we consider that the index table row is invalid and should be ignored.

![][image2]

The uncovered indexes would be a significant performance improvement for write intensive workloads. Also a common use case where uncovered indexes will be desired is the upsert select use case on the data table, where a subset of rows are updated in a batch. In this use case, the select query performance is greatly improved via a covered index but the upsert part suffers due to the covered index write overhead especially when the selected data table rows are not consecutively stored on disk which is the most common case.

As mentioned before, the DDL for index creation does not include the INCLUDE clause. We can add the UNCOVERED keyword to indicate the index to be created is an uncovered index, for example, CREATE UNCOVERED INDEX. 

As in the case of covered indexes, we can do read repair for uncovered indexes too. The difference is that instead of using the verify status for index rows, we would check if the corresponding data table row exists for a given index row. Since we would always retrieve the data table rows to join back with index rows for uncovered indexes, the read repair cost would occur only for deleting invalid index rows. Also, the existing index reverse verification and repair feature supported by IndexTool can be used to do bulk repair operations from time to time.

# Detailed Design

## Client Side Changes

### Parser

The Phoenix parser is updated with the addition of UNCOVERED keyword to the index create DDL statements. With this,  “CREATE UNCOVERED INDEX” is used to create uncovered global indexes. Also, the INCLUDE clause in the DDL statements is not allowed for uncovered indexes.

### Compiler

Currently, the Phoenix optimizer rewrites the query for a data table for indexes by replacing the data table name with an index table and remaining the columns referenced in the select statement using the index table column naming convention and then recompiles the query.

The uncovered columns result in a ColumnNotFoundException. Currently these expectations are handled only for local indexes and global indexes with the index hint. As part of this handling, the uncovered columns are tracked as the columns to be retrieved from the data table. As part of this design, we extend this behavior for uncovered global indexes.  

### Optimizer

The Phoenix optimizer will add the indexed columns to the set of columns to be retrieved from the data table to join with index rows. This means that even the indexed columns which are included in the row key of the index table will be treated as uncovered columns. This is required for two reasons. 

The first reason is to implement the overall uncovered index design read path where index table rows are verified against data table rows. To do this verification, we need to retrieve the indexed columns from the data table.

The second reason is to make this visible to the optimizer so that the optimizer does not prefer an index table over the data table or a covered index when all things are equal. Please note that the optimizer checks the size of the set of data columns to join with an index and prefers the table with the smaller set; and this set is empty for the data tables.

### Index Mutation Generation for Immutable Tables

The Phoenix client generates immutable index mutations on the client side within MutationState. The code will be updated so that the index mutations are generated for a single update on an uncovered index (instead of two-phase update). This is done for both delete and put mutations.

## Server Side Design

### Index Mutation Generation for Mutable Tables

The Phoenix client generates mutable index mutations on the server side within the IndexRegionObserver coprocessor. The code will be updated so that the index mutations are generated for a single update on an uncovered index (instead of two-phase update). IndexRegionObserver currently reads the table rows before generating index mutations. This behavior will be updated so that the read operation is skipped if the global indexes that would be updated by the batch are only uncovered indexes and the batch does not include an atomic upsert operation.

### Read Repair

The read repair for covered global indexes is currently performed by the GlobalIndexChecker coprocessor. For uncovered global indexes, the detection of repaired rows and their repair differ from those for covered indexes. The read repair for uncovered indexes will be integrated with the code path that joins the data table rows with index rows within UncoveredRegionIndexScanner.

## Integration Testing

Existing integration tests written for covered indexes will be updated to be also run uncovered indexes including the tests in BaseIndexIT, GlobalIndexOptimizationIT and UncoveredGlobalIndexRegionScannerIT.
